SVG vs Lottie vs GIF: Which Animation Format Should You Use?

Compare animated SVG, Lottie JSON, and GIF by editability, browser support, file behavior, and the job each format is good at.

Vekto EditorialNovember 2, 2026 7 min read

SVG, Lottie, and GIF can all show animation on a web page, but they are not interchangeable. SVG is a vector document, Lottie is a JSON animation format interpreted by a player, and GIF is a raster image sequence. The right choice depends on what you need to edit and where the animation will run.

Animated SVG for vector artwork

SVG stores shapes and paths as XML. That makes logos, icons, and simple illustrations crisp at different sizes. SVG can animate with SMIL or CSS and can be inspected or edited as markup. It is often a good fit for a small self-contained web animation, but SVG features and embedded animation should still be checked in the target browsers and tools.

Use animated SVG when you want scalable vector art and your delivery environment supports the animation features you need. If the file includes many complex filters or external references, test performance and portability before shipping.

Lottie for app and web players

Lottie packages animation data as JSON that a compatible player renders. It can preserve vector-like layers and keyframes across platforms, which is useful when a product team already has Lottie tooling. It also introduces a runtime dependency and a supported-feature boundary: not every After Effects or editor feature translates to every player.

Test the export with the exact Lottie player and version used by the product. Check loops, easing, image assets, and reduced-motion behavior.

GIF for broad, simple playback

GIF is a sequence of raster frames. It is widely previewable and simple to embed, but it does not preserve editable vector layers, has a limited palette, and can become large when the animation is detailed or long. For photographic motion, modern video formats are usually more suitable than GIF.

A quick decision: choose SVG for suitable vector artwork, Lottie for a compatible player workflow, and GIF only when its easy playback outweighs its raster and file-size limits. Keep an editable source no matter which file you deliver.
